blocks.title: Analogy: Adding on an Abacus Without Saying "Plus"
blocks.text: Like adding two numbers on an abacus by physically sliding beads and carrying overflow into the next column, without ever using the words "add" or "subtract", just physical movement and overflow handling.

blocks.caption: Compute a sum using only bitwise operations, no arithmetic plus or minus allowed

blocks.text: Negative numbers are represented in two's complement, and adding -1 and 1 correctly produces 0 once every bit, including the carry out of the highest bit, is handled consistently.
Before reaching for the plus operator out of habit, it helps to break addition down into the two things it actually does at the bit level: combining bits, and carrying overflow.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Adding two bits without carrying is exactly what XOR computes, since 0+0=0, 1+0=1, 0+1=1, and 1+1=0 (because 1+1 is 10 in binary, and the low bit of that is 0).

Observation 2: The carry that XOR misses happens only when both bits are 1, which is exactly what AND detects, and that carry always lands one position to the left, which a left shift produces.

Observation 3: So a full add is "XOR for the carry-free sum" plus "AND then shift left for the carry", and that carry itself might need to be added into the running sum, which means the same two steps can simply be repeated.

Observation 4: Since the carry can only ripple left through a fixed number of bit positions, this repetition is guaranteed to end once there is no carry left to propagate.

So this isn't really about avoiding the plus operator, it's about noticing that addition is just repeated XOR-and-carry until the carry runs out.
This XOR-and-carry framing is exactly the shortcut the optimized solution below uses, once you have seen why the slower brute force approach falls short.
Simulate addition the slowest possible way: repeatedly increment a by one, b separate times, using only a basic increment operation each time.

Return the final value of a.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Looping b times and incrementing a once per iteration directly simulates what addition means, one unit at a time, which makes correctness obvious even though it is slow.
The negative-b branch decrements instead of incrementing, since adding a negative number is the same as subtracting its absolute value.
This approach still technically depends on the built-in increment and decrement operators, which is why it does not fully satisfy the spirit of solving this without addition or subtraction.

blocks.text: Repeated incrementing eventually reaches the correct sum, though it technically still relies on increment and decrement operations that are themselves a disguised form of addition and subtraction.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(b), proportional to the magnitude of b, extremely slow for large values.
Space: O(1), only the running value is kept.

Limitation: this is both slow for large values and philosophically still uses addition and subtraction under the hood through the increment and decrement operators, which does not genuinely demonstrate an addition free approach.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why brute force is limited: it loops proportionally to the magnitude of b, and for large values this is extremely slow, plus it secretly reuses increment and decrement, which are themselves addition and subtraction in disguise.

What it wastes: it processes one unit of value per iteration instead of processing all bit positions in parallel.

Can we avoid the wasted work: yes. XOR combines every bit position's carry-free sum in one operation, and AND then shift left produces every carry in one operation too.

Can the results combine into one step: yes. Repeating "XOR for sum, AND-shift for carry" until the carry is zero converges in at most 32 rounds, bounded by the fixed bit width, not by the value of b.

Addition can be broken into two independent parts using pure bitwise operations: XOR of a and b gives the sum of every bit position ignoring any carrying, and AND of a and b, shifted left by one, gives exactly the carry that needs to be added into the next higher position. Treating that carry as a new value to add back in, and repeating this XOR-and-carry process, converges to the final sum once the carry becomes zero.
Repeatedly compute the carry free sum via XOR and the carry via AND shifted left, until the carry disappears.

blocks.caption: Optimized: XOR for the carry free sum, AND shifted left for the carry, repeat until no carry remains

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), bounded by the fixed bit width of the integers, since the carry can propagate at most that many positions.
Space: O(1), only a couple of running values are kept.

XOR correctly computes the sum of two bits whenever at most one of them is 1, since in those cases there is no carry to produce. The only case XOR gets wrong on its own is when both bits are 1, where the true sum is 10 in binary, a carry into the next position; AND detects exactly this case, and shifting left moves that carry into the correct next bit position. Repeating this process folds every carry back in until none remain, at which point the XOR result is the true, fully carried sum.

items: a ^ b computes the sum of every bit position as if there were no carrying, which is correct everywhere except positions where both bits were 1.
(a & b) shifted left by 1 finds exactly those both-1 positions and moves them one place left, since that is where their carry belongs.
Reassigning a to the XOR result and b to the shifted carry, then looping, keeps folding any remaining carry back in until b becomes 0 and no carry is left.

blocks.text: This problem is the classic demonstration that XOR performs addition without carrying, and AND followed by a left shift computes exactly the carry, together fully reconstructing addition from purely bitwise primitives.

items: Forgetting to mask values to 32 bits in languages without fixed width integers, which can let intermediate values grow unexpectedly during the carry loop.
Not handling negative numbers carefully, since their two's complement representation must flow through the exact same XOR and carry logic without special casing.
Assuming the loop always runs a fixed number of times regardless of input, when really it stops as soon as the carry reaches zero, which can happen well before 32 rounds.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["One of the two values is 0","The loop terminates immediately since there is no carry to propagate"],["Adding a positive and a negative number that sum to exactly 0","The two's complement based carry logic handles this correctly without any special casing"],["Both values are negative","Two's complement representation means the same XOR and carry rules still apply unchanged"]]}

items: State the two rules explicitly before coding: XOR performs addition ignoring carries, AND shifted left computes exactly what needs to be carried, since naming both rules up front makes the repeat-until-no-carry loop much easier to follow.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If they say "you cannot use plus or minus", think XOR for the carry-free sum and AND then shift for the carry.
If they say "can you avoid looping proportional to the value", think about why the carry-based approach only needs at most 32 rounds.
If they ask "how does this handle negative numbers", think two's complement, since XOR and AND behave consistently on the underlying bit pattern regardless of sign.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(b) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (XOR and carry): O(32) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: XOR for carry-free addition, AND shifted left for the carry
Core Idea: Addition is XOR (bit sum without carry) plus AND-shifted-left (the carry), repeated until no carry remains
Time: O(32) for the optimized solution, O(b) for brute force
Space: O(1) in both approaches
Most Important Observation: a full addition is just XOR-and-carry repeated until the carry disappears
Interview Difficulty: Intermediate, a strong test of comfort with bitwise carry propagation
One-line memory trick: XOR adds without carrying, AND-shifted-left finds the carry, repeat until there isn't one
